cards.lore: The general wrote a clean, readable memoir acting like a neutral observer of his own continental slaughter.
cards.power: Third-Person Gaslighting. Play to rewrite an opponent's successful turn as a catastrophic failure. They must accept your version of reality.

cards.lore: The most famous opening line in military memoir history is just a fancy way of saying 'I came to conquer all three.'
cards.power: Geographic Pretext. Divide the game board into top, bottom, and middle. Opponent must not exist in each.

cards.lore: Institutional assessments can treat corpses as logistics. The Gauls are treated as terrifying as the Romans need to justify the math.
cards.power: Institutional Math. Delete half the opponent's deck. Call it 'Pacification.'

cards.lore: The specific institutional memory of the Celtic world was all written down. When the Romans burned the groves, they deleted the hard drive.
cards.power: Unwritten Memory. Hide three cards in your pocket. The opponent cannot forget what they cannot prove existed.

cards.lore: Rome's primary client tribe learned the hard way that a Roman alliance has limits military pressure will eagerly expose.
cards.power: Strategic Defection. Switch alliances mid-game. Take all your current ally's resources with you.

cards.lore: A genuine demographic migration that Caesar intercepted, creating the perfect pretext for a war of total conquest.
cards.power: Demographic Avalanche. Move 380,000 tokens at once. Burn your base so you can't retreat.

cards.lore: The wealthy plateau tribe whose status resentment over losing top-dog status made the pan-Gallic revolt its political urgency.
cards.power: Displaced Pre-eminence. Gain +5 Attack if you are currently losing. The anger is on your side.

cards.lore: The aristocrats loved the Roman patronage; the people knew it was just an elaborate leash.
cards.power: Grassroots Sabotage. Disable the opponent's highest-value aristocratic card using mob rules.

cards.lore: Caesar called them the bravest because they were furthest from Mediterranean luxury and fought the Germans for fun.
cards.power: Barbarian Distance. Immune to 'Civilizing' effects. The further from the center you play them, the harder they hit.

cards.lore: They used terrain and timing to hit the Romans before formations could be completed, nearly ending Caesar's career in an afternoon.
cards.power: Camp Ambush. Attack while the opponent is still shuffling their deck.

cards.lore: The chieftain who earned a client's trust to bait fifteen Roman cohorts out of winter camp and straight into the meat grinder.
cards.power: Fatal Trust. Convince an opponent to discard their hand to 'avoid a trap,' which is the actual trap.

cards.lore: The Gauls who went East. They had no druid tradition, not a reputation for ferocity that terrified Hellenistic kings into hiring them.
cards.power: Mercenary Range. Play this card on any opponent's board. They fight for whoever pays the most attention.

cards.lore: He built a genuinely pan-Gallic coalition, figured out the correct strategy, and lost because marginally better is enough for Rome.
cards.power: Tragic Sacrifice. Surrender this card to save your remaining deck. The opponent gets to gloat for 6 turns.

cards.lore: The Senonian chieftain who sacked Rome and summarized all asymmetric negotiation with five syllables: Vae Victis.
cards.power: Heavy Sword. When you score a throw, your sword on the scales. You win.

cards.lore: The British chieftain who refused to give the Romans the heavy infantry fight they wanted, opting to spend their day with chariots.
cards.power: Mobile Skirmish. Never lock into combat. Deal damage and return this card to your hand immediately.

cards.lore: The politician who understood Caesar was a permanent guest, not a guest, and was killed trying to escape the hostage tour.
cards.power: Refusal to Cross. Cancel any forced-play effect. You die, but you don't have to.

cards.lore: They weren't just religious specialists; they were the command layer, the legal arbitrators, and the institutional memory.
cards.power: Divine Exemption. This card cannot be attacked. It directs all your other cards and makes the violence 'legitimate.'

cards.lore: The only Druid Caesar named. His cooperation was structurally necessary for the Roman client system to function in Gaul.
cards.power: Theological Legitimation. Force an opponent to agree with your move because 'the gods (or the Senate) said so.'

cards.lore: You don't sell your professional credentials. The head contains the soul; taking it transfers the enemy's power to the victor.
cards.power: Cedar-Oil Trophy. When you defeat an enemy card, pin it to your board. It generates four points every turn.

cards.lore: The pan-Gallic druidic council met here. Rome burned it and built a cathedral on top. But the spring remembers.
cards.power: Subterranean Memory. Long after your cards are destroyed, they still produce +1 Resource from the discard pile.

cards.lore: They fought without armor as a deliberate ritual choice, communicating that normal survival mathematics did not apply to them.
cards.power: Survival Mathematics. Attack with zero defense. Your opponent takes psychological damage just watching you go.

cards.lore: The tall bronze trumpet with the animal head. Its harsh, discordant shriek was the specific signal that activated the Roman fear response.
cards.power: Acoustic Terror. Opponent must skip their next turn with their cards facing away from them.

cards.lore: The twisted gold neck ring. Armor for the soul. A library of accumulated honor, and the ultimate trophy for a Roman looter.
cards.power: Honor Advertising. Place on a unit. If defeated, the opponent gets double points. If victorious, you get triple.

cards.lore: Not an archery platform. A mobility tool for the elite warrior who fights on foot but needs the prestige of a drive-by arrival.
cards.power: Aristocratic Extraction. Save one of your defeated cards right before it dies by pulling it back to your hand.

cards.lore: 90 centimeters of metallurgical superiority designed for slashing. Romans claimed they bent; archaeologists claim Romans lied.
cards.power: Open Melee. Devastating in open space, but loses power if the opponent clusters their cards together.

cards.lore: The heavy thrusting weapon that gave the naked Gaesatae their name. Big, iron, leaf-shaped, and terrifying.
cards.power: Socketed Impact. Pierce through an opponent's shield card and hit the unit behind it.

cards.lore: Everyone's weapon. The specific equipment the farming warrior carries from his fields to the battlefield and back.
cards.power: Farmer's Reach. Can be equipped by any low-level card to instantly make them a ranged threat.

cards.lore: A personal tool for individual combat, unlike the Roman Scutum. It reflects an honor-based system, not a collective-discipline machine.
cards.power: Individual Block. Block an attack, but you cannot form a shield wall with other cards.

cards.lore: The Gauls invented it. The Romans wore it. Medieval knights get the credit. Historiography is just organized theft.
cards.power: Technological Adoption. When an opponent uses a new tactic, copy it immediately and claim you invented it.

cards.lore: From simple caps to spectacular winged parade helmets. The metallurgical sophistication was so high, Roman auxiliary units just wore the local gear.
cards.power: Ceremonial Distraction. Equip to draw all enemy attacks to this unit, because it looks absolutely fabulous.

cards.lore: Vercingetorix's doctrine: destroy your own grain to break the Roman supply chain. The hardest part was convincing the tribes to do it.
cards.power: Resource Denial. Burn your own resource deck. The opponent immediately starves and loses half their hand.

cards.lore: The moving city of the Helvetii turned into an impromptu fortress at Bibracte, proving that migrating badgers do not go down easily.
cards.power: Mobile Fortress. Turn your discard pile into a defensive wall. It takes three turns to breach.

cards.lore: The Gauls wrapped around the unsecured Roman flank. The strategic psychology of a whole empire was born in this panic.
cards.power: Exposed Flank. Attack the card on the far edge of the opponent's board for double damage.

cards.lore: They weren't conquering barbarians stumbling into an empty city. They conducted a seven-month siege and extracted maximum leverage.
cards.power: Capital Siege. Occupy an opponent's territory. They pay you gold every turn until you leave.

cards.lore: Woe to the conquered. Brennus's response when the Romans complained about the scales. The permanent truth of every asymmetric negotiation.
cards.power: Absolute Leverage. Change the win conditions of the game while you are currently winning.

cards.lore: The Romans caught a Gallic army between two consular armies. The last tactical expression of the naked warrior charge in Italy.
cards.power: Pincer Movement. Trap a unit in the space between two of your own to instantly destroy it.

cards.lore: The Helvetii nearly broke the legions. Caesar claimed victory, marched them home, and wrote the first chapter of his PR masterpiece.
cards.power: Narrative Management. Even if you lose the battle, you get to write the score sheet.

cards.lore: The Roman regiment that hit the Nervii from the flank just as Caesar was grabbing a shield and looking for a life in the front lines.
cards.power: Flank Rescue. Play instantly when you are about to lose. Save your board and score out the attackers.

cards.lore: Caesar attempted to take Dumnorix to Britain as a hostage. Standard Roman operating procedure: hold their kids, take their land.
cards.power: Political Extortion. Steal an opponent's card. If they attack you, you rip it.

cards.lore: The one town the Gallic council refused to burn. Caesar took it, used its grain, and continued the campaign. Sentimentality is a vulnerability.
cards.power: Fatal Sentimentality. Refuse to destroy one of your own resource cards. The opponent captures it and wins the game.

cards.lore: Fifty kilometers of earthworks. Fighting on two fronts simultaneously. The most terrifying engineering flex in military history.
cards.power: Double Walls. Build a wall facing your opponent, and a wall facing the rest of the room. You can't move, but neither can they.

cards.lore: 250,000 warriors from across Gaul, assembled to break the Roman perimeter. They failed by the thinnest of margins.
cards.power: Mass Coordination. Combine the attack power of every single card in your deck for one Turn. If it fails, you lose instantly.

cards.lore: Caesar personally rode along the line with cavalry to stabilize the collapsing perimeter. The final engagement lasted a day and a night.
cards.power: Absolute Commitment. Exhaust your entire hand to add +1 to a crucial roll.

cards.lore: Caesar kept Vercingetorix in a cell for six years just to parade him in his triumph. The ultimate political communication.
cards.power: Cruel Display. Keep a defeated leader on your board for six turns before discarding it, just to demoralize the opponent.

cards.lore: Gallic barrel logistics moved the Roman army. The technology survived; the culture that produced it was reclassified as 'barbarians.'
cards.power: Logistics Hack. Store unused resources indefinitely.

cards.lore: The Celtic metallurgical mastery that allowed chariots and wagons to conquer rough terrain. Rome rode on Gallic rims.
cards.power: Frictionless Advance. Move your cards twice as fast across the board.

cards.lore: The Gallic invention that fed Europe for a thousand years. Caesar destroyed the druids, but he kept the bread-makers.
cards.power: Endless Sustenance. Generate +1 food token every turn forever.

cards.lore: Caesar's response to Ambiorix's trap: the systematic, complete destruction of a tribe, written down with bureaucratic indifference.
cards.power: The Erasure. Remove a faction from the rulebook entirely.

cards.lore: FrizzleBob notes that the sentence that begins the conquest is written in the language of the conqueror. Time to edit.
cards.power: Rule Vandalism. Cross out any printed rule on an opponent's card and write your own.

cards.lore: If it looks designed or corporate, damage it. The truth lives in the messy, chaotic, unhinged margins.
cards.power: Gutter Attack. Your margin doodles come alive and eat the opponent's resource tokens. If it looks designed or corporate, damage it. The truth lives in the messy, chaotic, unhinged margins.

cards.lore: The Roman system was a rigid machine. The FrizzleBob system is a pair of scissors and zero respect for institutional boundaries.
cards.power: Cut & Paste. Physically cut one of your cards in half to double its number of units, halving its health.

cards.lore: The druids are gone. The cathedral was built. But the water still flows beneath it. Vae victis.
cards.power: Permanent Haunting. You win the moral victory. The game ends in a draw, but the opponent feels bad about it.
